I posted another question to AskVoat today about the details of the One Vote Per Public IP anti-voting manipulation policy (or what ever it’s called) and how it works for people behind a shared public IP address (i.e. NAT): https://voat.co/v/announcements/comments/87919

The responses included a lot of people suggesting that this policy is flawed, while also acknowledging that there needs to be some method to prevent people from gaming the voting system with multiple accounts. There were only a few different suggestions for alternate methods.

Atko had listed a few possible alternate methods here: https://voat.co/v/announcements/comments/87919/151938 (thanks user/sn1ke)

What’s your suggestion for how to prevent a single user from voting with multiple accounts?

For the other methods, what’s wrong with them? i.e. they disenfranchise too many people or they are too easy to game, etc. The trick for Voat will be find a system that balances the two.

Note, I’m not asking about potential voting formulas such as weighting, or ways to prevent group voting.
What your suggestion for an anti-voting manipulation mechanism?

Some of the methods suggested so far (first four are Atko’s):

“in order to vote, have every account be whitelisted by phone number verification (not within my student budget, may happen in a year or two)”

  • Privacy concerns. Especially for users in countries with authoritative regimes (or a DHS)

“in order to vote, have every account be whitelisted by photo ID verification (nobody would ever want to do this)”

  • like he said, no one would ever want to do this

“in order to vote, have every account be whitelisted by a $5 payment for voat premium subscription (doable, very few people would want to do this)”

  • still easy to game. Any politician or company could create hundreds of voting accounts for a couple thousand bucks.
  • entry barrier for people from countries where $5 is real money?

“uniquely identify people by analyzing various elements (desktop resolution, user agent etc), (not doable for our current time constraints, this is a student sideproject, not a large organization with dozens of senior developers with free time on hand)”

  • overly complicated. Especially since it can still be gamed (as can any of these).

Current system: one public IP address, one vote.

  • NAT is very, very, very common and it’s not going anywhere anytime soon. In some cases (schools and businesses) there are hundreds of users behind single IP address. In other cases entire countries can be behind a single IP address. And they all share a single vote.

Combination of public and private IP addresses.

  • can still be gamed with users who have multiple devices or virtual machines.
  • could be a fair balance between not disenfranchising huge chunks of users and limiting voting with multiple accounts.
  • fairly simple to implement

Browser based limitations (e.g. cookies, browser fingerprinting, etc )

  • probably too easy to run multiple instances of multiple browsers on a single machine.

IPSec VPN

  • difficult to implement, complicated for users, and scaling will be an issue

Wait for IPv6 which will allow every device to have their own public IP address and no more NAT’ing.

  • wide spread adoption of IPv6 is years away, and may never become dominant. NAT’ing solved many of the reasons for IPv6 and there’s no pressure for users, sites or applications to end support IPv4; as long as every site/applications supports IPv4 there no reason for users to migrate to IPv6, as long as all users are on IPv4, there’s no reason for sites/applications to migrate to IPv6.

Honestly, the current method is the most scalable (outside of not tracking), and while unfair for people behind shared IP's it is difficult to game consistently. Facebook implements a solution for likes that is based on browser cookies, and as mentioned, that is really easy to game. If Voat becomes bigger, there may be companies that come along and attempt to game the system for money in similar ways that they do for Facebook. This is probably never going to happen, unless Voat starts to hit the top hundred websites.

Uniquely identifying people based on slight changes on their system is a decent method that is already widely implemented in tracking programs used by advertising and analytics companies. While I am personally not a fan of this method, it is decent, proven, reliable, and fast if done correctly.

Cookies are decent, easily bypassed, Physical limitations(Money, phone, photo ID) are impractical, and IPv6 is being adopted slowly.

I say fuck it. If someone cares enough to go to the slight trouble of creating multiple accounts for giving multiple imaginary internet points, I say let 'em. It's not like they matter for anything. If they do it so much that they get caught, they get banned; otherwise, meh.

What about larger cases? Not all cases of vote manipulation will be trivially small or unimportant.

What about an entity with a botnet that gradually comes to control hundreds of accounts? If I had such a system in place, I could rent my services to companies with a vested interest in this or that kind of topic being up or downvoted. Or a government could use such a system to manipulate the visibility and apparent community approval of certain kinds of political content, or news about government actions.

Vote manipulation will be very important here if the site continues to grow. It's a huge deal on Reddit.

If anything, referral tracking might be best besides the public IP method. Track where the votes come from (no referral is odd - copy-paste, and lots of referrals from one place is also odd - brigading)
